insight.title: What holds the clouds in place
insight.subtitle: A quiet study of the invisible weight drifting above us.

sections.text: We look up and see white puffs drifting through the blue. They look like tufts of cotton or soft pillows of steam. You might think they weigh next to nothing. Yet, a single summer cloud can carry over a million pounds of water. It floats above your head, massive and silent, waiting for the wind.

How does something so heavy stay so high? The secret is in the heat. As the sun warms the earth, the air rises in gentle, invisible columns. These warm breaths act like giant hands. They cradle the tiny droplets, keeping them aloft. Gravity pulls, but the rising warmth provides a soft, constant lift.

This invisible balance happens every single day. It reminds us that there is a quiet strength in the air we breathe. Even when things feel light and effortless, there is often a great weight being held with grace. Life is full of these hidden miracles. We just have to remember to look up.

news.title: Long-read whole genome sequencing uncovers new genetic variants linked to autism
news.description: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have identified new genetic variants associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) by using long-read whole genome sequencing (LR-WGS), an emerging approach that reads large sections of the genome at once, making it easier for scientists to find new genetic variants and understand how genetic variants affect the function of a gene.

news.title: Light-guided evolution creates proteins that can switch, sense, and compute
news.description: Researchers have created a method called optovolution that uses light to guide the evolution of proteins with dynamic behaviors. By engineering yeast cells so their survival depended on proteins switching states at the right time, scientists could rapidly select the best-performing variants. The technique produced new light-sensitive proteins that respond to different colors and improved optogenetic systems. It even evolved a protein that behaves like a tiny logic gate, activating genes only when two signals are present.
